n: The psalm opens by remembering a past blessing: God showed favor to his land and restored Israel’s fortunes. Many think this refers to the return from Babylonian exile.

f.g: Restored the fortunes; brought back the exiles.

n: God forgave his people and covered every sin.
He withdrew all his anger and turned from his fury.
Now a new plea: restore us again, God of our salvation, and end your displeasure with us. The return from exile was hard, and they need renewal again.
Will you be angry with us forever, across every generation?
Won’t you revive us again so your people can rejoice in you? Revival leads to joy.
Show us your loyal love, Lord, and give us your salvation.
Now the psalmist listens for God’s answer: God speaks peace to his faithful people — but they must not go back to foolishness.

f.w: I will hear what God the LORD will speak
he will speak peace unto his people

n: God’s salvation is close to those who reverence him, so that his glory may dwell in the land again — as it did in the temple.

f.w: that glory may dwell in our land

n: A beautiful image: God’s loyal love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss. Qualities that might seem opposed — mercy and justice — embrace. Many see this fulfilled in Christ’s Atonement.

f.w: Mercy and truth are met together
righteousness and peace have kissed each other

n: Truth springs up from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven. Latter-day Saints often connect this verse with the coming forth of the Book of Mormon from the ground and revelation from heaven in the Restoration.

f.w: Truth shall spring out of the earth
righteousness shall look down from heaven

n: The Lord will give what is good, and the land will produce its harvest.

f.w: our land shall yield her increase

n: Righteousness will walk ahead of God like a herald, preparing a path for his steps.
